title: Domain-Driven Design Fundamentals
summary: The core DDD mindset — modeling software around the business domain and a shared language, so the code stays easy to change as the business itself changes.

slides.markdown:
[Hexagonal and Clean Architecture](hexagonal-and-clean-architecture) tell you where the boundary goes and which direction dependencies point. They deliberately say nothing about **what goes inside the core** — how to actually model an order, a subscription, or a claim as code.

Domain-Driven Design (DDD), coined by Eric Evans, answers that question. Its central bet: software is easiest to change over time when its structure mirrors how the business actually thinks about the problem, using the business's own words, not a generic set of database tables and getters/setters.

This topic covers the mindset. The next topic, Tactical DDD Patterns, covers the concrete building blocks — entities, value objects, aggregates — that this topic introduces at a conceptual level.

slides.subTitle: Software that mirrors the business is easier to change
slides.markdown:
Most software eventually diverges from the business it serves — the business grows new rules, exceptions, and terminology, and the code, built around a generic "CRUD over a database" shape, has nowhere natural to put them. Each new rule becomes a special-case `if` bolted onto a controller or a stored procedure, because the code was never structured around business concepts in the first place.

DDD's bet is that if the code's structure — its classes, their names, their boundaries — mirrors the business's own model of the problem, then a business change maps to a localized code change instead of a scavenger hunt. When a product manager says "a subscription can now be paused, not just cancelled," a DDD-modeled codebase has an obvious place for that: the `Subscription` entity gains a `pause()` method. A generic CRUD codebase has to figure out which of a dozen files touching `subscriptions` need to change.

slides.subTitle: One vocabulary shared by domain experts and code
slides.markdown:
DDD's foundational practice: agree on a **single vocabulary** for domain concepts, used identically by business stakeholders in conversation and by engineers in code — class names, method names, even variable names.

If the business calls it a "claim," the code has a `Claim` class, not a `Ticket` or a `Case` that engineers privately mapped to "claim" in their heads. If the business distinguishes an "authorized" payment from a "captured" one, the code has both states named exactly that, not a single generic `status` string with values `"auth"` and `"capture"` that only engineers know how to read.

The test for whether ubiquitous language is actually being followed: sit a domain expert next to the code (or a diagram of its class names) and see if they recognize their own vocabulary. If engineers have privately renamed things "for clarity" and the business wouldn't recognize the terms, the language has already forked — and every future conversation between the two groups now requires a mental translation step, which is exactly the friction DDD exists to remove.

slides.subTitle: Objects with identity that persists across state changes
slides.markdown:
An **entity** is an object defined by a continuous identity, not by its current attributes. A specific `Order` is the same order whether its status is `pending`, `shipped`, or `refunded` — every field on it can change, and it's still that order, tracked by an identifier (an order ID) that never changes.

This matters for equality: two `Order` objects with an identical ID are the same order even if one has stale data loaded, while two `Order` objects with *different* IDs are different orders even if every other field happens to match byte-for-byte (say, two customers who both ordered the exact same items on the exact same day). Entity equality is **identity equality**, not field-by-field equality — and getting this backwards is a common source of subtle bugs, like accidentally merging two distinct customers' orders because a naive equality check compared their line items instead of their IDs.

slides.subTitle: Defined by their attributes, immutable, no identity
slides.markdown:
A **value object** is the opposite: it has no identity at all, and it's fully defined by its attributes. `Money(amount=50, currency="USD")` and another `Money(amount=50, currency="USD")` created separately are simply **equal** — there's no sense in which they're "the same instance" that matters, the way there is for two references to the same `Order`.

Value objects are typically made immutable: instead of mutating a `Money` object's amount in place, you create a new one (`price.add(tax)` returns a new `Money`, it doesn't mutate `price`). This eliminates a whole category of bugs where one part of the code holds a reference to a value object and is surprised when another part mutates it underneath.

Common value objects: `Money`, `Address`, `DateRange`, `EmailAddress`, `PhoneNumber` — anything where "which specific instance" is meaningless and only "what does it contain" matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Entity vs. value object, side by side
slides.markdown:
Take a `Customer` (entity) placing an `Order` that ships to an `Address` (value object):

| | Customer (entity) | Address (value object) |
|---|---|---|
| **Defined by** | A stable customer ID | Its street, city, postal code fields |
| **Two instances with identical fields** | Still two different customers if IDs differ | The same address, full stop |
| **Mutability** | Mutates over time — same customer, new email, new tier | Typically immutable — a changed address is a new `Address`, not the old one edited |
| **Equality check** | Compare IDs | Compare all fields |

A customer who changes their shipping address hasn't become a different customer — the `Customer` entity's `shippingAddress` field just now points at a different `Address` value object. The entity's identity is untouched; only one of its attributes, itself a value, was swapped out.

slides.sectionTitle: The domain model as executable knowledge
slides.markdown:
DDD treats the domain model as more than a data schema — it's meant to be **executable knowledge about the business**, where the model's structure and behavior encode real rules, not just storage shape.

A `Subscription` class with a `pause(until: Date)` method that internally checks "can't pause a subscription already in its final billing cycle" *is* a piece of business knowledge, expressed as code that runs and can be tested. Compare that to a `subscriptions` database table with a `status` column and the same rule enforced ad hoc wherever a pause request happens to be handled — the knowledge exists, but it's scattered and unenforceable by the type system.

The practical difference shows up when the rule needs to be relied on: calling `subscription.pause(date)` and trusting it either succeeds or raises a clear domain error is fundamentally more reliable than trusting that every caller remembered to re-check the same condition themselves.

slides.subTitle: Data bags with logic living elsewhere
slides.markdown:
The most common DDD failure, common enough to have its own name: the **anemic domain model**. Classes are named after domain concepts — `Order`, `Subscription`, `Invoice` — but contain only fields and getters/setters, with zero behavior. Every rule about what an order can or can't do lives in a separate `OrderService` full of static-feeling functions that take an `Order` and poke at its public fields.

This looks like DDD on the surface — the class names match the ubiquitous language — but it has none of the actual benefit. The knowledge ("can't cancel a shipped order") isn't attached to the thing it's about, so nothing stops a different part of the codebase from setting `order.status = "cancelled"` directly and skipping the check entirely. Real DDD puts the rule *on* `Order` itself (`order.cancel()` that internally validates), so the invariant can't be bypassed by reaching into the object's fields.

slides.sectionTitle: A value object and an entity, in code
Domain experts and engineers modeling together
slides.markdown:
DDD isn't purely a coding technique — Eric Evans frames it as much as a **collaboration practice** as a set of patterns. The ubiquitous language is built through actual conversation between domain experts (underwriters, claims adjusters, logistics planners — whoever understands the business deeply) and the engineers who'll encode it, not by engineers reading a requirements doc alone and guessing at vocabulary.

A common technique for this is **event storming**: get domain experts and engineers in a room, and map out the business process as a sequence of domain events ("order placed," "payment authorized," "inventory reserved") on sticky notes, before writing a line of code. This surfaces vocabulary disagreements early — a moment where the sales team says "cancelled" and the fulfillment team means something subtly different by it — while it's cheap to resolve, instead of after two systems have already been built around incompatible assumptions.

Entities and value objects are the smallest building blocks. On their own they don't yet answer questions like: what stops two related entities from being saved in an inconsistent state relative to each other? Who's responsible for loading a `Subscription` and its related billing history as one unit?

That's exactly what Tactical DDD Patterns covers next — aggregates, aggregate roots, repositories, and domain events, which compose entities and value objects into consistency boundaries you can actually build a system around.
